person.name: Steve_Jobs
person.summary: Steve Jobs co-founded Apple with Steve Wozniak and led the company through the personal-computer revolution. After founding NeXT and acquiring Pixar, he returned to Apple to oversee products including the iMac, iPod, and iPhone.

portrait.caption: Stylized portrait based on a historical source image
portrait.creator: AI generated artwork

conclusion: Steve Jobs helped bring personal computers to a mass consumer market through Apple and the Macintosh. After returning to Apple, he led the company behind the iMac, iPod, and iPhone. Pixar became a leading animation studio under The Walt Disney Company.

events.title: Birth in San Francisco
events.description: Paul Jobs worked as a repossession agent in San Francisco. Clara Jobs worked as a bookkeeper. After Clara had an ectopic pregnancy, the couple sought to adopt a child. They promised to pay for Jobs’s college tuition.

closed adoption.explanation: A closed adoption keeps identifying information and contact between the birth and adoptive families confidential.

events.title: Leaves Reed College
events.description: Paul and Clara Jobs paid the tuition despite the strain on their finances. Jobs withdrew after one semester. He remained at Reed College in Portland, Oregon, to audit selected classes, including Robert Palladino’s calligraphy course.
events.background:
Reed College was the only school to which Jobs insisted on applying in September 1972. The private college in Portland cost more than Paul and Clara Jobs could comfortably afford. Jobs had met Chrisann Brennan at Homestead High School, and their relationship continued while he was in Oregon. At Reed, he became friends with Robert Friedland, then the student-body president. Friedland later owned the All One Farm commune in Oregon. Daniel Kottke, another Reed undergraduate, became a close friend there.

After leaving the degree program, Jobs stayed in the Reed community without a dormitory room. He slept on the floors of friends’ dorm rooms. He returned Coke bottles for food money. He also walked to the local Hare Krishna temple for its weekly free meals. These years brought him into contact with the counterculture around the college and with Zen Buddhism, which he and Brennan began practicing through the Zen teacher Kōbun Chino Otogawa.

The letterforms he studied at Reed supplied a design concern that computer makers usually treated as secondary. Jobs later recalled learning about serif and sans-serif typefaces, varied spacing between letter pairs, and the visual proportions of type. When the Macintosh was designed, he said those lessons led to multiple typefaces and proportionally spaced fonts. In his 2005 Stanford commencement address, he described the later computer as the first with that combination of typographic features.

events.title: Searches India for Enlightenment
events.description: Jobs traveled through India with his Reed College friend Daniel Kottke to seek spiritual instruction. They visited Kainchi, a religious retreat associated with Neem Karoli Baba. They then traveled to a retreat associated with Haidakhan Babaji after finding Kainchi nearly deserted.

events.title: Founds Apple Computer
events.description: Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne formed Apple Computer Company as a partnership in Los Altos, California. Wayne drafted the original partnership agreement. Jobs and Wozniak formed the company to develop and sell Wozniak’s [[Apple I|Apple I computer]].

Apple I.explanation: The Apple I was an early personal computer designed by Steve Wozniak. Jobs and Wozniak founded Apple to develop and sell it to computer hobbyists.

events.background:
In 1975, the Homebrew Computer Club gave Bay Area hobbyists a place to trade designs and ideas about small computers. Wozniak was designing calculators at Hewlett-Packard when he completed the basic Apple I design. Jobs had already learned that small electronic devices could be sold through the blue boxes he and Wozniak made for free long-distance calls. The first plan was to sell bare Apple I circuit boards to hobbyists for $50 each. Wozniak sold his HP scientific calculator to help finance the first batch. Jobs sold his Volkswagen van. Daniel Kottke later recalled that he was the only person regularly working in the Crist Drive garage. Wozniak arrived about once a week with new code. Jobs spent long hours in the kitchen calling potential investors.

Computer retailer Paul Terrell ordered 50 fully assembled Apple I machines for $500 each. His Byte Shop had a reputation for slow payment. Jobs obtained a $15,000 line of credit for the parts needed to fill the order. The credit alarmed Wayne because each member of a partnership was personally responsible for its debts. Wayne had assets that creditors could seize. He had spent a year repaying debts after his slot-machine manufacturing business failed in 1971.

Wayne prepared the Apple I Operations Manual and drew detailed circuit diagrams that enabled the circuit-board artwork to be made for larger production. He also created the company’s first logo, Apple Newton, which pictured Isaac Newton under an apple tree. Wayne’s inventory and documentation methods from Atari were adapted for the new company. Twelve days after the partnership began, he filed an amendment withdrawing from it and accepted $800 for his stake. Wozniak later said that Wayne stayed for a few months. In January 1977, Apple became a corporation with funding and credit arranged by Mike Markkula.

events.title: Introduces the Apple II
events.description: The Apple II appeared at the West Coast Computer Faire in San Francisco. Steve Wozniak designed the computer. Steve Jobs directed its molded plastic case and presented it as a consumer product ready for use.

images.caption: Apple II computer on museum display
images.creator: Marcin Wichary

events.title: Launches the Macintosh
events.description: Steve Jobs introduced the Macintosh at Apple’s annual shareholders meeting in Cupertino, California. He had taken over the project from Jef Raskin. He presented the computer at De Anza College.

images.caption: Steve Jobs with Macintosh computer, January 1984
images.creator: Photo: Bernard Gotfryd - Edited from tif by Cart

event_class.title: Macintosh
event_class.description: A personal computer combines a graphical user interface, mouse control, display, keyboard, and compact all-in-one case for general consumers.
event_class.impact: The Macintosh helped launch desktop publishing in 1985 when Apple added the LaserWriter printer and Aldus PageMaker software became available.

events.title: Leaves Apple to Found NeXT
events.description: Apple’s board backed John Sculley’s reorganization plan and removed Steve Jobs from his operating role. Jobs resigned from Apple on September 17, 1985. He founded NeXT with five former Apple employees. NeXT developed computers for higher-education and business customers.

images.caption: NeXT Cube computer
images.creator: Michael Hicks from Saint Paul, MN, USA

events.title: Acquires Pixar
events.description: Steve Jobs bought Lucasfilm’s computer graphics division and established it as the independent company Pixar. Jobs became Pixar’s chairman and majority shareholder. Pixar specialized in computer hardware and animation.
events.background:
Computer-generated imagery was still an unusual part of feature animation when Lucasfilm’s computer division employed John Lasseter. Lasseter had trained in the Character Animation program at the California Institute of the Arts. Disney animators Jack Hannah and T. Hee created the program. His teachers included Disney veterans Eric Larson, Frank Thomas, and Ollie Johnston. Fellow students included Brad Bird, John Musker, Henry Selick, Tim Burton, and Chris Buck. Lasseter made Lady and the Lamp in 1979 and Nitemare in 1980. Each short won a student Academy Award for Animation.

Lasseter joined Walt Disney Productions after graduating in 1979. Disney had reviewed about 10,000 portfolios during its late-1970s talent search. The studio selected about 150 apprentices. About 45 remained permanent employees. Lasseter worked on an intended sequence called The Emperor and the Nightingale for the uncompleted Disney project Musicana. The work later contributed to the development of Fantasia 2000. Disney dismissed Lasseter after he promoted computer animation. He then joined Lucasfilm and worked with computer-generated imagery there.

The new company retained Lasseter as a creative force while it pursued computer hardware and animation. Lasseter eventually directed Toy Story in 1995. He also directed A Bug’s Life, Toy Story 2, Cars, and Cars 2. Toy Story received a Special Achievement Award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. Lasseter won an Academy Award for the animated short Tin Toy. He oversaw Pixar films and associated projects through 2018. Five animated films he executive-produced later earned more than $1 billion each worldwide, including Toy Story 3, Frozen, Zootopia, Finding Dory, and Incredibles 2.

events.title: Marries Laurene Powell
events.description: Steve Jobs met Laurene Powell after she spoke with him at a Stanford Business School lecture in October 1989. Powell was an MBA student. They married in Yosemite National Park on March 18, 1991. Zen monk Kōbun Chino Otogawa conducted the Buddhist ceremony.

events.title: Returns to Apple
events.description: Apple acquired NeXT in December 1996, bringing Steve Jobs back to Apple. In July 1997, Apple appointed him interim chief executive in Cupertino, California. The company faced falling sales and a weakened product line.

events.title: Unveils the iMac
events.description: Steve Jobs introduced the iMac in Cupertino, California, with industrial designer Jony Ive. The display and computer shared one translucent case. The machine was designed for internet access.

events.title: Introduces the iPod
events.description: Steve Jobs presented the iPod at Apple’s headquarters in Cupertino, California. The iPod was Apple’s new portable music player. It worked with [[iTunes]], Apple’s software for organizing digital music.

event_class.title: iPod
event_class.description: A hard-drive digital music player uses a scroll wheel and iTunes synchronization to organize and carry thousands of songs.
event_class.impact: The iPod creates a major new consumer electronics business for Apple.

iTunes.explanation: iTunes was Apple software for organizing, playing, and synchronizing digital music with devices such as the iPod.

events.title: Receives Cancer Diagnosis
events.description: Steve Jobs learned that he had a [[pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor]]. He initially pursued dietary and alternative treatments for the condition.

pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.explanation: This tumor begins in hormone-producing cells of the pancreas. It differs biologically from the more common pancreatic cancers that begin in pancreatic ducts.

events.title: Reveals the iPhone
events.description: Steve Jobs introduced the iPhone at the Macworld Conference and Expo in San Francisco. He presented it as a mobile phone, a widescreen iPod, and an internet communications device.

images.caption: First public showing of the Apple iPhone
images.creator: ArnoldReinhold

event_class.title: iPhone
event_class.description: A touchscreen mobile device combines telephony, web browsing, music playback, software applications, and multi-touch controls in one handheld computer.
event_class.impact: The iPhone establishes Apple as a major maker of smartphones and mobile software platforms.

events.background:
Apple entered 2007 with the iPod and iTunes already giving it a large presence in digital music. The company’s hardware group had also spent years developing compact products around a close working relationship between Jobs and Jony Ive. Apple’s earlier handheld Newton had failed in the 1990s. The new project put a phone, music player, and web device into a category where physical keyboards, small displays, and carrier-controlled software were standard.

The presentation depended on a live demonstration. Jobs moved through music, photographs, web pages, maps, email, and a phone call on a large screen behind him. He used a touch interface built around gestures such as swiping and pinching. Ive joined the demonstration by telephone. The call made Ive the first person to speak publicly with Jobs through the new device. Jobs also placed a prank call to a Starbucks store, ordering 4,000 lattes before ending the call.

## Software and sales

Apple’s first model went on sale in the United States on June 29, 2007. It initially ran software supplied by Apple and did not offer the later App Store for independent software makers. The company announced in 2007 that it would support third-party applications the following year. The App Store opened in 2008 alongside iPhone OS 2.0.

The first iPhone reached one million sales after 74 days. It was sold through an exclusive arrangement with AT&T in the United States. Apple later extended the line into a platform for mobile software and services. Ive continued to lead Apple’s industrial design work on the iPhone and its successors.

background_images.creator: Blake Patterson

events.title: Resigns as Apple CEO
events.description: Steve Jobs told Apple’s board that he could no longer meet his duties as chief executive. He asked the board to appoint Tim Cook as his successor. Jobs remained chairman of the board.
events.background:
Apple had already arranged for Tim Cook to run day-to-day operations during an earlier medical leave in 2009. In January 2011, the board approved a third medical leave for Jobs. Cook again took charge of daily operations. Jobs continued to make most major decisions during the leave. His public appearances became rare. He introduced the iPad 2 in March and appeared at Apple’s Worldwide Developers Conference in June. Apple had become a company with about $100 billion in annual revenue by the time of the leadership change. Forbes contributor Robin Ferracone wrote in September that Jobs and Cook had helped take Apple from $11 billion in revenue in 1995 to less than $6 billion in 1998, then to $100 billion in 2011.

In his letter to Apple’s board, Jobs invoked a standard he said he had set for himself. He wrote that he would be the first to let the board know if he could no longer meet Apple’s expectations and duties. He wrote, “Unfortunately, that day has come.” He also said he believed Apple’s “brightest and most innovative days” lay ahead. The letter named Cook as the person Jobs recommended to lead the company. The board acted that day.

Cook had joined Apple in 1998 after working for IBM, Intelligent Electronics, and Compaq. At Apple, he closed factories and warehouses and shifted production to contract manufacturers. His operations group cut inventory from months to days. It also made long-term advance investments in flash memory beginning in 2005. Those contracts secured supplies for the iPod Nano, iPhone, and iPad. Cook had become chief operating officer in 2007. He had already served as acting chief executive during Jobs’s absences.

Apple’s leadership passed to Cook six weeks before Jobs died from complications of pancreatic cancer on October 5. In 2012, Cook reorganized the executive team after the troubled release of Apple Maps. Scott Forstall left his position overseeing iOS, and responsibilities were distributed among other senior executives, including Jony Ive.

events.title: Dies in Palo Alto
events.description: Jobs’s health declined after his cancer returned. He died at his Palo Alto home with his wife, Laurene Powell Jobs, and family members nearby.

event_class.place_of_rest: Alta Mesa Memorial Park, Palo Alto
